evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In 2025, we wrote extensively about how datacenter capacity was the bottleneck for AI compute growth. By early 2026, the datacenter supply situation improved considerably, but it became clear that chip production was now the limiting constraint. Now – mid-way through the year – it is clear that financing will now be one of the most significant obstacles to ramping large scale compute broadly available to everyone.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says data-center capacity was the AI-compute bottleneck in 2025, chip production became the limiting constraint by early 2026, and financing was a major constraint by mid-2026.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: This is why Nvidia has stepped in and has started backstopping GPU rental offtakes themselves . In the backstop program, Nvidia provides a take-or-pay commitment to Neoclouds – a minimum revenue guarantee on the underlying GPU capacity. In exchange for this backstop, Nvidia also shares in a portion of the Neocloud’s revenue earned above the backstop level.
evidence.one_line: Nvidia has started a program providing Neoclouds take-or-pay minimum-revenue guarantees on GPU capacity and sharing in revenue above the backstop level.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Nvidia’s backstop program is typically six years in length, and during these six years, Nvidia stands ready to purchase compute at pre-agreed price levels that vary over the time period.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says Nvidia's backstop program typically covers six years, with Nvidia ready to purchase compute at pre-agreed prices that vary over the term.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Each Neocloud is expected to negotiate the backstop terms individually, and we can expect that different Neoclouds may end up with different revenue share and backstop schedules.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis expects Nvidia to negotiate backstop terms individually, with schedules and revenue shares varying by Neocloud.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: The below table is an illustrative example to explain the basic terms of the program – we present a backstop pricing curve that we believe to be on the lower end of the backstop range – in this case at an average of $2.36 over the six-year period, but we expect that most Neoclouds will negotiate higher backstops.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis's illustrative lower-end Nvidia backstop schedule averages $2.36 over six years; it expects most Neoclouds to negotiate higher backstop levels.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In the first scenario, the Neocloud focuses on a customer base that rents at a 1-year or lower tenor, so we model the 1-year rental price for a GB300 starting at $6.75/hr for the first year before decaying over time as the overall market cost of compute declines.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models GB300 one-year rental pricing at $6.75 per hour in year one, declining over time, for its short-tenor scenario.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: As with any business that is operating a “curve trade” – that is investing long and renting out on shorter tenors – we should expect that in theory the average realized rental price over the project lifetime should be slightly higher than the current 6y fixed price of ~$4.00.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis expects average realized rental prices over a short-term-rental project's life to be slightly above the current six-year fixed price of about $4 per hour.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In the case where Nvidia earns 40% revenue share, we see that in year 1, the Neocloud will charge its customers $6.75/hr on average. Of this, the Neocloud earns the full amount up to Nvidia’s year 1 backstop of $3.68/hr, but for the difference between $6.75/hr charged to customers and the $3.68/hr backstop amounting to $3.07/hr, Nvidia will earn $1.23/hr and the Neocloud will earn $1.84/hr. In total, the Neocloud will realize $5.52/hr for the first year, which of course is lower than the $6.75/hr that they would have earned without the backstop.
evidence.one_line: In SemiAnalysis's illustrative year-one case, a 40% Nvidia revenue share on the $3.07-per-hour rental amount above a $3.68 backstop yields Nvidia $1.23 per hour and the Neocloud $1.84 per hour above the backstop, for $5.52 per hour total Neocloud revenue.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Over the six years of this scenario, the Nvidia take rate works out to be about 18% on average, but without the backstop, there would be no cluster!
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis's six-year short-tenor scenario implies an average Nvidia revenue take rate of about 18%.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: It is important to highlight that while Nvidia does have meaningful internal compute needs, neither Nvidia or the Neoclouds have any intention of using the backstop, and thus it is not surprising that the backstop levels would result in a typical Neocloud earning a zero or slightly negative project IRR.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says neither Nvidia nor Neoclouds intend to use the backstop and that modeled backstop-level rentals would give a typical Neocloud zero or slightly negative project IRR.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: When they do, they need to evaluate debt service coverage ratios in the scenario in which the backstop is triggered to determine how much funding can be provided.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says lenders sizing loans against Nvidia-backed clusters evaluate debt-service coverage assuming the backstop is triggered.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: We see that the short-term 1y rental book scenario clearly offers the best IRR among the backstopped scenarios at 25.4%, and these IRRs could realize even higher if the rental market turns out to be strong enough such that 1y and shorter rental rates decay by less than we modeled in the curve below.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models a 25.4% IRR for a backstopped one-year rental-book scenario, with potentially higher returns if short-term rates decline less than modeled.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: As expected, the IRRs are higher without a backstop – reaching as high as 40.7% when renting for 1y tenors with no backstop.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models up to a 40.7% IRR for one-year rentals without a backstop.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: But if Neoclouds activate the backstop and rent to Nvidia at those prices, they can expect to earn zero or negative IRRs.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says Neoclouds renting to Nvidia after activating the backstop would earn zero or negative IRRs in its modeled scenario.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Readers may notice the huge gap between CoreWeave 5y unsecured bonds at ~10% and the 5.9% that CoreWeave paid for the fixed-rate tranche of their DDTL 4.0 $8.5B delayed-draw term loan, which was backstopped by Meta. This 5.9% yield works out to about 90 basis points wider than Meta’s 5y bond yield of ~5.0%. This can be interpreted as the market pricing CoreWeave’s execution risk with respect to that particular project at 90bps.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis reports CoreWeave's Meta-backstopped $8.5 billion DDTL 4.0 fixed-rate tranche carried a 5.9% yield, versus about 10% on CoreWeave five-year unsecured bonds and about 5.0% on Meta five-year bonds; it interprets the spread over Meta at about 90 basis points as project execution risk.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: To fund a cluster that they intend to rent on shorter terms with a broad book of customers, a Neocloud would have to fall back on unsecured funding. For a top Neocloud, this would mean paying an additional 4% interest, which would significantly impact the economics of the deal given the 70-80% loan to value ratios used to finance GPUs.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis estimates unsecured funding costs a top Neocloud about four percentage points more in interest, against GPU-financing loan-to-value ratios of 70–80%.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: In our modelling, we show that increasing funding from an all-in cost of 5.62% to an all-in cost of 10% drops PBT margins from 14.8% down to only 5.4%.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis models PBT margins falling from 14.8% to 5.4% when all-in funding costs rise from 5.62% to 10%.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Unsecured lending to a top Neocloud would probably be around 10%, but expect even more expensive unsecured financing for smaller Neoclouds with a shorter track record.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis estimates unsecured lending to a top Neocloud would likely cost about 10%, with higher costs for smaller, less-established Neoclouds.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: When it comes to the Nvidia backstop, banks look at the DSCR ratios assuming revenue earned under the scenario where the backstop is activated. They are looking for a DSCR of at least 1.3x, particularly for the first few years of GPU financing agreement and size their loans to ensure that this bar is met. This typically corresponds to a 70-80% loan to value (LTV) ratio.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says lenders typically require at least 1.3x DSCR, especially in the first years of Nvidia-backed GPU financing, corresponding to 70–80% LTV.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis
evidence.event_time: First years of GPU financing agreement

evidence.quote: We think that initial lending will be at a wider spread than the current 5y backstopped hyperscale deals which come in at around SOFR + 225bps (roughly equivalent to a Z-spread of 195bps, or about 5.9% total yield) but at a tighter spread than CoreWeave’s 5-year unsecured corporate bond which has a yield of ~10% (roughly equivalent to Z-spread of 600bps).
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis expects initial Nvidia-backstopped Neocloud lending to price wider than hyperscale-backstopped loans at SOFR plus 225 basis points (about 5.9% yield), but tighter than CoreWeave's five-year unsecured bonds at about 10%.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis

evidence.quote: Nvidia’s backstop program is only getting started, and we see announcements coming faster every quarter. Many Neoclouds are already deep in negotiations with Nvidia, and there are still others that are considering engaging with the backstop program.
evidence.one_line: SemiAnalysis says Nvidia's backstop program is at an early stage, expects announcements to accelerate quarterly, and reports many Neoclouds are in advanced negotiations while others are considering participation.
evidence.speaker: SemiAnalysis
